name: Erik Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a workday sound like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play saxophone with a dance orchestra, record simple horn guides and teach four adult players. I have a music degree and twenty-eight years of paid band work. I like when the floor keeps dancing through a quiet sax break; I dislike being asked to fix a guide track for free.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work support home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner earns a regular wage at a library and our children are grown. We own a small flat, have nine months of expenses saved and my fees are high for this job. There are many local bands, though a new seat still needs an opening. I use AI daily to draft date lists and label takes, then check them against signed calls and my own recordings.

say: I'd welcome **faster lists** with paid rehearsals and dances intact.
I'd say an **automatic label** cannot hear my late sax entrance.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and partner wage cover one moved dance.
The **shows and pupils** should keep paying in mild AI.
do: Confirm **six paid dances** and four pupils; request written guide revision fees.
Check **AI dates and labels** against signed calls/recordings and save a fifth of extra cleared festival fees after essentials.
feel: I feel **calm** while paid calls and household wages hold.
S0.quote: An automatic label cannot hear whether my sax came in behind the singer.
fieldNote: His **high musician fees** and nine-month reserve buffer one delayed dance payment.
Daily **AI lists and labels** are existing use, checked against signed calls and his recordings.

steps.text: Confirm six paid dances and four pupils; request written guide revision fees
Check AI dates/labels; save fifth of extra cleared festival fees after flat charges, food and reeds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra a faster list helps if every paid rehearsal and dance stays on it. An automatic label cannot hear whether my sax came in behind the singer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nine months saved and my partner's regular wage cover a moved dance. If AI only tidies lists, I expect our booked shows and teaching to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm six paid dances and four pupils and request written revision fees for the guides. In the first year of this mild change I'll keep checking daily AI dates and take labels against signed calls and my recordings, and save a fifth of extra cleared festival fees after flat charges, food and reed costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm while the paid calls stay signed. One late fee would be inconvenient, not a threat to the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with a guide revision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A buyer asked for a third horn-guide take last spring and had no revision line in the contract. I sent an invoice anyway and waited six weeks to be paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust an automatic take label?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a take label is not proof the music is right. I listen to the sax line myself before sending a file.

think: Guides bring **one fifth** of my own pay.
Our **nine-month reserve** buys time, not a permanent replacement for orders.

Listen **against the original**; stop note errors/leakage and require written consent before other audio.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost guide orders despite search time.
S1.quote: I learn new tools quickly, but a clean saxophone tone is not a signed recording order.
fieldNote: His **new AI trial** needs paid instruction outside shows, owned nameless audio and commercial-use permission.
He **listens manually** and stops for note errors or files leaving approved storage.

steps.text: Compare ten guide invoices and seek paid engineer lesson outside booked dances

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the bandleader that generated horn guides could replace small recording orders. I'd ask for live playing and revision fees in writing before the next dance season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guides bring about a fifth of my own pay, and clients could stop buying them. Nine months saved and many bands nearby give me time to find paid live work, but the missing fifth would still count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare ten guide invoices with new orders and pay attention to a new AI tone checker, which flags unsteady notes in a recording, after a paid lesson from the band engineer. In the first year I'll test only my own nameless sax take under the band's paid-use licence and approved local storage, listening against the original and stopping if a note changes or audio leaves the band; I'll keep all booked dances and pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic reduction in guide fees. I learn new tools quickly, but a clean saxophone tone is not a signed recording order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The band must pay the engineer and licence, and the lesson must not replace a paid show. Otherwise I'll keep checking the take by ear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you test with a pupil's solo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't test with a pupil's solo. Their voice or instrument audio would need written permission and an agreed storage rule first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra that thinking AGI by 2028 could make horn guides before a robot plays saxophone. Playing robots follow around 2031, so I want our live dance dates signed now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide orders to end in 2028, taking a fifth of my pay. Live dances could also thin later, but that is a separate risk while the current season is booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total guide pay, request signed paid dance dates and ask for actual pension statements before discussing a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if live dances also fall, I'll seek a posted paid band-tutor role only if my music degree and teaching experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the last bus works; I'll keep orchestra and pupils until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected fifth of my pay disappearing. Nine months saved and many local bands let me search; I would feel worse if live work collapsed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a band-tutor job open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No band has offered me a tutor chair. I would read a current paid posting and its teaching requirements before I count any wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen our pension figures. Nine months saved is useful, but it will not pay an unknown retirement bill forever.

say: I'd price a **first-steps saxophone group** during the warning years.
I'd demand **signed costs** for room and insurance before taking places.
think: A class must pay **my teaching and preparation**, not just room hire.
do: Offer **saxophone group** after written hire/cost/insurance and six fees cover room/sax-hire/inspection/insurance/cleaning/reeds/my teaching/preparation/travel outside paid calls.
Inspect **six loan saxophones** or sound own instruments; defer/refund everyone below six safe paid places.
Renew **after 2031** only with six safe full-cost fees and written terms; keep booked dances and pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** until paid places cover every class cost.
S3.quote: A saxophone group of willing learners is not a paid job if hall hire and my preparation eat the takings.
fieldNote: The **separate group** prices room including inspected saxophone loans, insurance, cleaning, reeds, teaching/preparation and travel outside current paid calls.
The **six-place floor** requires safe saxophones and full-group refund for low enrollment or equipment failure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the hall that five years to AGI by 2031 lets me price a separate saxophone first-steps group. Playing robots follow around 2034, and I would want the room and insurance costs signed before taking a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may cheapen horn guides before 2031. I can teach an adult's first reed and breath, but a class that misses my own teaching fee is only a hobby with rent attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll get written room hire, cost and insurance terms before deposits for a four-week adult saxophone group on an afternoon free of booked dances and pupils. Six adults must prepay enough for room including inspected loan saxophones, insurance, cleaning, personal reeds, my teaching, preparation and travel; the hall keeper must inspect six loan saxophones or adults bring sound instruments. In the first year after 2031 I'll renew only with the same six full-cost safe paid places and written terms; if fewer pay or an instrument fails without replacement, I'll defer and refund the whole group while keeping booked music work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious until six real fees pay the whole class. A saxophone group of willing learners is not a paid job if hall hire and my preparation eat the takings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the loan saxophones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The keeper must check pads, keys and mouthpiece cleaning before any learner plays. If one safe place fails, I refund everyone unless another sound instrument makes six again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this replace a paid dance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the group is on an open afternoon. I won't cancel a paid dance or one of my four pupils to fill a speculative class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 lets us read real pension figures and paid dance contracts. Saxophone-playing robots follow around 2039, but the bill for our flat comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still want to teach and play. Nine months saved and steady household pay help now, but I cannot call retirement funded without a pension amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid dance-call plan, then save a fifth of each extra cleared festival fee after flat charges, food and reed costs toward twelve months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid dances and pupils while booked and continue the separate saxophone group only on free afternoons with six safe fees covering room including inspected loan saxophones, insurance, cleaning, personal reeds, my teaching, preparation and travel under written terms; otherwise I'll defer and refund everyone. I'll slow paid work only if actual pension and booked fees cover the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant work while today's bookings and nine months saved are sound. I will read the pension statement before deciding how many dance dates to give up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra festival pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no extra festival pays, no money from it moves to savings. I won't shift food money to make twelve months appear on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen the pension amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we have not seen the pension amount. I would compare the actual figure with our regular bills before dropping a booked show.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because paid horn guides could end before another role opens. Signed dance dates, actual pension figures and a posted qualified tutor job with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid when a saxophone group fills a hall. Six learners on a list are not six safe paid saxophone places.

headlineQuote: Six learners on a list are not six safe paid saxophone places.
portrait: Erik is a **58-year-old experienced saxophonist** with a music degree, partner and grown children.
His **higher pay**, nine-month reserve and many nearby bands provide room to respond to recording losses.
He uses **AI daily** for lists and takes, learning a new checker only with paid instruction and safe owned audio.
He tests a **separate saxophone group** only with six safe full-cost paid places and written room/insurance terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase one fifth of Erik's pay from horn guides.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed dance calls**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying tutor work with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
